questions.corrige_markdown: A **joint** is a **place where two or more bones meet** (articulate).

questions.enonce_markdown: Name four types of synovial (movable) joints found in the human body. *(4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four types of synovial joints (with an example of each):

1. **Ball-and-socket joint**: shoulder and hip joints.
2. **Hinge joint**: elbow, knee and finger joints.
3. **Pivot joint**: between the atlas and the axis (neck, allows the head to turn).
4. **Gliding (plane) joint**: between the carpals of the wrist and between the tarsals of the ankle, and between the vertebrae.

questions.enonce_markdown: Draw a well labelled diagram to show the structure of a typical synovial joint. *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Diagram to be drawn by the candidate: a longitudinal section through a synovial joint, with a title (e.g. "Longitudinal section through a synovial joint") and ruled label lines.*

**What to draw:** the **ends of two bones** that meet, **separated by a small space (the synovial cavity)**; a **layer of articular cartilage** covering the end of each bone; the **synovial membrane** lining the capsule, and the **synovial fluid** filling the cavity; the **fibrous (joint) capsule** surrounding the joint and joining the two bones; **ligaments** joining the bone ends on the outside.

**Labels expected:** bone (two), articular (hyaline) cartilage, synovial cavity, synovial fluid, synovial membrane, capsule (fibrous capsule), ligament. Optionally: tendon and muscle.

**Functions to remember:** cartilage reduces friction and acts as a shock absorber; synovial fluid lubricates the joint; ligaments hold the bones together; the capsule encloses and protects the joint.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe how movement is brought about at the elbow joint. *(10 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **elbow is a hinge joint** between the **humerus** (above) and the **radius and ulna** (below). It allows movement in **one plane only** (bending and straightening the arm). Movement is brought about by a pair of **antagonistic muscles**, the **biceps** (on the front of the upper arm) and the **triceps** (at the back), acting on the bones, which work as a **lever** with the elbow as the **fulcrum**.

- Muscles are attached to bones by **tendons**. The biceps is attached to the **radius** (and to the scapula), and the triceps is attached to the **ulna** (and to the humerus and scapula). **Ligaments** join the bones together at the joint, and **synovial fluid** lubricates it.
- Muscles can **only pull (by contracting), never push**, so two muscles are needed to give movement in two directions.
- The muscles contract when they receive **nerve impulses** from the brain.

**Flexion (bending the arm):** the **biceps contracts** and the **triceps relaxes**. The biceps pulls the radius upwards, so the forearm is **raised** towards the upper arm.

**Extension (straightening the arm):** the **triceps contracts** and the **biceps relaxes**. The triceps pulls the ulna backwards, so the forearm is **lowered and straightened**.

The contraction of one muscle (the **prime mover or agonist**) and the relaxation of the other (the **antagonist**) is what produces smooth, coordinated movement.
